theme: Vanity of vanities; the futility of wisdom and pleasure
readingInstruction: Read Ecclesiastes 1:1-2:26. The tone changes sharply from Proverbs. Read slowly, and let the Preacher’s honesty about life sink in. Do not rush to resolve it.
settingTheScene: Ecclesiastes is the book of the Preacher (Hebrew Qoheleth), “the son of David, king in Jerusalem,” traditionally taken to be Solomon. If Proverbs says that wisdom leads to life, Ecclesiastes asks what happens when life seems not to add up. The key word is “vanity,” literally “breath” or “vapor.” The Preacher explores life “under the sun,” that is, as seen from a purely earthly viewpoint, and comes back with hard truths. This is the second book of the wisdom collection, and it is an honest companion to Proverbs.
observation: “Vanity of vanities, says the Preacher, vanity of vanities! All is vanity” (1:2).
“What does man gain by all the toil at which he toils under the sun?” (1:3).
“A generation goes, and a generation comes, but the earth remains forever” (1:4).
“What has been is what will be, and what has been done is what will be done, and there is nothing new under the sun” (1:9).
“For in much wisdom is much vexation, and he who increases knowledge increases sorrow” (1:18).
He tries pleasure, laughter, wine, great works, wealth, and music (2:1-8).
“Then I considered all that my hands had done… and behold, all was vanity and a striving after wind” (2:11).
“There is nothing better for a person than that he should eat and drink and find enjoyment in his toil. This also, I saw, is from the hand of God” (2:24).
interpretation:
The first line stuns the reader: “Vanity of vanities! All is vanity.” The word “vanity” (hebel) means a breath, a vapor, something that cannot be grasped. The Preacher is not saying that life is meaningless in every way, but that it is fleeting and elusive, impossible to hold. His starting question is: what does a person gain from all his work? If all work ends in death and is forgotten, what is the point?

He observes nature: the sun rises and sets, the wind circles, the streams run to the sea, and nothing is ever finished. History repeats. There is “nothing new under the sun.” The human heart is not satisfied by seeing and hearing. These lines describe the weariness of life without a larger purpose.

In chapter 2, the Preacher conducts an experiment. He tries pleasure, laughter, wine. He builds houses and gardens, gathers silver and gold, and has everything his eyes desire. And at the end of it, “Behold, all was vanity and a striving after wind.” He does not deny that these things are enjoyable. He says they cannot satisfy. Wisdom is better than folly, as light is better than darkness, but the same fate comes to both. The wise man dies like the fool.

This is a painful honesty. The Preacher does not offer easy answers. He lays out the problem: a life lived only for what this world offers, even in the best circumstances, ends in frustration. Death is the great leveler.

But the chapter ends with a hint of something else: “There is nothing better than that he should eat and drink and find enjoyment in his toil. This also, I saw, is from the hand of God.” Enjoyment is possible, but only as a gift received from God, not as something grasped. This is the first note of a theme that runs through the book.
connection: Paul says that creation was “subjected to futility” in hope of liberation (Romans 8:20-21), echoing the Preacher’s vanity. Jesus asked, “What does it profit a man to gain the whole world and forfeit his soul?” (Mark 8:36). In Christ, our labor “is not in vain” (1 Corinthians 15:58). Jesus is the one who gives the satisfaction that nothing under the sun can: “Whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never be thirsty” (John 4:14).
application:
Ask what you are chasing that cannot satisfy. Be honest.

Receive one ordinary joy today (a meal, a conversation) as a gift from God’s hand.

Do not rush past the question of futility. Let it drive you to Christ.
prayerPrompts: Tell God what you tend to chase that leaves you empty.
Ask him to satisfy you in himself.
Ask him to teach you to receive eating, drinking, and work as gifts.
